newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italy parties discuss welfare reform.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italy parties discuss welfare reform.

text.p: Political parties supporting Italy's centre-left government met on Monday to discuss plans to reform the welfare state and one official said that, apart from the hard left, positions were close.

Fabio Mussi, lower house leader for the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), said that the centre-left "Olive Tree" coalition parties were broadly in line and hoped to find agreement with the Marxist-inspired Communist Refoundation party.
"The points of view in the Olive Tree coalition are very, very close if not identical," he told reporters. "Now the hope is to find agreement with Refoundation as well."
"On the subject of social security and pensions there is still a certain disagreement (with Refoundation)," Mussi added.

Italy is under pressure to carry out a convincing reform of social spending -- and to shake up its pensions system -- to prove that public finances will be kept under control before the planned 1999 launch of the single European currency.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi opened talks last week with Italy's three main union confederations, trade bodies and employers' group Confindustria on the thorny question of reforms of the welfare state and Italy's generous pensions system.
Monday's meeting was aimed at working out a common document by the centre-left majority on welfare reforms.
A document, to form the basis for discussions, was presented by the government to unions and employers last Wednesday and was slammed by both unions and Refoundation.
Sergio Cofferati, head of the CGIL union, said at the time that the document was inadequate and that a strike might be inevitable if the government did not adopt common positions.

Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti, whose party provides the coalition with its majority in the lower house of parliament and was at Monday's meeting, said last week that the document was a "false start".

Mussi said the draft document worked on by the centre-left coalition was not hugely different to that presented by the government but some elements had been added, particularly regarding employment and training.
The leader of the employers' body Confindustria Giorgio Fossa and CISL union head Sergio D'Antoni had earlier made clear that they regarded the government as the sole mediator in the negotiations.

The Prodi document called for a review of a generous early retirement system which allows Italians to draw a pension based on the length of service rather than because they have reached retirement age, questioning whether the country could afford it.
